title: Taught is not learned
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart criticises the common primary assessment practice of giving teachers a grid of objectives for each year group to tick off or colour in. Such grids, he says, record what has been taught, not what has been learned, so coverage becomes a poor proxy for attainment. Because the whole curriculum cannot be assessed, any assessment is a sample of the domain, and the real question is which parts to sample. He offers three criteria for choosing key performance indicators: threshold concepts that permanently change how pupils see a subject, prerequisite knowledge that later learning depends on, and common misconceptions. He answers the worry about curriculum narrowing by insisting on strong curriculum leadership and quality assurance of breadth, and recommends pitching some KPIs above age-related expectations through application and transfer rather than acceleration. Finally he argues that a few KPIs assessed repeatedly over time give a better basis for judgement than a single check soon after teaching.
points: Tick-list and RAG-rated grids tell you what was taught, not what pupils have learned, because coverage is a weak proxy for learning.
Since a full curriculum cannot be assessed, assessment should deliberately sample the domain with a small set of well-chosen KPIs.
Good KPIs are threshold concepts, prerequisite knowledge or common misconceptions, and ideas like place value qualify on more than one count.
Limiting the number of assessed items is not curriculum narrowing provided leaders guard the breadth of what is taught.
Assessing a few KPIs repeatedly over the year respects how learning and forgetting work and builds teachers' assessment literacy.
quotes: If you have an assessment system that requires teacher judgement of every objective taught, the best you’ll get from tick lists or RAG rated grids is an indication of what has been taught, not what has been learned. Coverage is a poor proxy for learning.
The entirety of the curriculum cannot be assessed. It would take at least as long to assess it as it would to teach it. As such any assessment is based on a sample of the domain.
These are things that future learning relies upon and without which children would not be able to access upcoming curriculum intent.

Having a small number of KPIs per subject per year is not an argument for curriculum narrowing. The curriculum still needs to be broad and balanced but teachers make inferences about attainment in the entire domain from a sample of it.
This is bound up in the idea that children who grasp ideas quickly are challenged through depth, not acceleration to content in subsequent years.

Learning happens over time through multiple interactions, time to forget and in different contexts. So having fewer KPIs assessed regularly is a better indicator of learning than assessing once, soon after teaching and assuming that performance will stick.

A small number of carefully chosen KPIs assessed regularly over the year provides a basis for better judgement than a grid of every objective taught. And it also nudges teachers into better assessment literacy, that we can only ever sample the domain and that learning happens over time.
